> Five modules, building from "what is a model" to "should I have used one".

## About this section

Section 1 argued that method choice follows from the question. This section
teaches the methods themselves — enough to use them, and enough to know when
not to.

Every module uses real data. Where a method is a poor fit for the data we have,
we say so rather than pretending otherwise.

## The five modules

| | Module | Core idea |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | [Foundations of Machine Learning](1-foundations.qmd) | Train/test splits, overfitting, why a baseline comes first |
| 2 | [Supervised Learning](2-supervised-learning.qmd) | Classification, and why accuracy misleads |
| 3 | [Unsupervised Learning](3-unsupervised-learning.qmd) | Clustering and dimensionality reduction; finding structure that isn't there |
| 4 | [Deep Learning & Sequence Models](4-deep-learning.qmd) | What neural networks buy you, and what they cost |
| 5 | [LLMs in Research](5-llms-in-research.qmd) | Using AI assistants without damaging your science |

## How to read this section

The modules are cumulative. Module 1's train/test discipline is assumed
everywhere after it.

::: {.callout-important}
## A running theme
Each module ends by asking whether a simpler method would have done as well.
Surprisingly often the answer is yes. That is a real result, not a failure.
:::

## Prerequisites

R and the `tidyverse`. If you worked through the exercise in Section 1, you
have the conceptual grounding you need.

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "here"))
```

::: {.callout-note}
